title: Acrisol

definition.text: A WRB reference soil group of strongly weathered soils with low-activity clays, in which exchangeable aluminium exceeds the exchangeable base cations.

facts.text: Acrisols are linked to humid tropical and subtropical climates, such as Brazil's, and often carry forest.
In USDA soil taxonomy they match the Humult, Udult and Ustult suborders of the Ultisols, plus Oxisols with a kandic horizon and some Alfisols.
Most Ultisols are classed in the WRB as either Acrisols or Alisols.
Low fertility and toxic aluminium limit farming, so many Acrisols are used for forestry, low-intensity pasture or protected areas.
Where climate allows, tea, rubber, oil palm, coffee and sugar cane can be grown on them.
Infertile Acrisols make up most of the 'common soil' that surrounds the Amazon's fertile terra preta patches.

prerequisites: World Reference Base for Soil Resources

title: Alisol

definition.text: A WRB reference soil group of acidic soils with high-activity clays, in which exchangeable aluminium exceeds the exchangeable base cations.

facts.text: Alisols have a clay-enriched argic horizon with a high cation exchange capacity, but low base saturation in the subsoil.
Their clays are far more active than those of Lixisols, Acrisols and Ferralsols, and they tend to lie on younger or more geologically active terrain.
They occur in tropical and humid subtropical climates and also in temperate regions.
Farming them needs lime and fertiliser, they erode easily, and at their low pH aluminium and manganese dissolve and can poison intolerant plants.

prerequisites: World Reference Base for Soil Resources

title: Andosol

definition.text: A WRB reference soil group of soils formed in volcanic ash and other tephra, rich in allophane or in complexes of aluminium and organic matter.

facts.text: The name comes from Japanese an, 'dark', and do, 'soil'; it is a synonym of kuroboku.
Andosols develop in glass-rich parent material: while much volcanic glass remains they are called Vitric, and as the glass weathers they gain andic properties.
Acidic tephra in humid climates yields aluminium-organic complexes (Aluandic Andosols); basic tephra or dry climates yield allophane and imogolite (Silandic Andosols).
Both kinds hold much ferrihydrite and have a bulk density of 0.9 kg/dm3 or less.
Andosols cover about 1–2% of Earth's ice-free land, mostly around the Pacific Ring of Fire, from Chile and Mexico to Japan, Java and New Zealand.
Silandic Andosols are very fertile unless phosphorus is fixed; wet rice on Java's Andosols feeds some of the world's densest populations.
In USDA soil taxonomy many Andosols are Andisols, though some fall in the Inceptisols.
Fossil Andosols far from today's volcanoes have been dated as far back as the Precambrian, 1.5 billion years ago.

prerequisites: World Reference Base for Soil Resources

title: Anthrosol

definition.text: A WRB reference soil group of soils formed or heavily changed by long-term human use, such as irrigation, added organic waste or paddy-field cultivation.

facts.text: Anthrosols can form from any parent soil and are common where people have farmed for centuries.
In north-western Europe they commonly have plaggic or terric horizons built up with manure, together covering some 500,000 hectares.
Telltale signs include high phosphate from bones, tissue or excrement, dark colour, high pH from added wood ash, and buried tools or waste.
Qualifiers record the cause: plaggic (long manuring), irragric (flood or surface irrigation), hortic (deep cultivation and kitchen waste), anthraquic (man-made water management such as terracing).
Archaeologists use Anthrosols, spotted by eye or even from satellite images, to find sites of long-term habitation.
Rich in minerals and decayed organic matter, Anthrosols are good for farming, and well-managed ones act as a carbon sink.
Similar soils go by many national names, among them plaggen soils, paddy soils, terra preta, Agrozems in Russia and Anthroposols in Australia and Canada.

prerequisites: World Reference Base for Soil Resources
contested_note: Because Anthrosols vary so widely in composition and structure, there is debate over whether they should be an independent soil group.
notes: Contested sentence S:646dfb7546e8 (cites 1996) states the debate directly.

title: Calcisol

definition.text: A WRB reference soil group of soils with a substantial secondary accumulation of lime (calcium carbonate).

facts.text: Calcisols are common on calcareous parent materials and widespread in arid and semi-arid lands; they were formerly called Desert soils and Takyrs.
They develop mostly in alluvial, colluvial and wind-blown deposits of base-rich weathering material, on level to hilly land.
Natural vegetation is sparse: drought-adapted shrubs and trees and short-lived grasses.
Dryness, stoniness or a shallow petrocalcic horizon limit farming, but irrigated, drained and fertilised Calcisols can be highly productive.
Many occur alongside Solonchaks that are in fact salt-affected Calcisols.
Their total area may be some 10 million square kilometres, almost all in the arid and semi-arid subtropics.
Most USDA Aridisols fall into the Calcisols, Gypsisols, Durisols and Solonchaks of the WRB.

prerequisites: World Reference Base for Soil Resources

title: Cambisol

definition.text: A WRB reference soil group of moderately developed soils at the beginning of soil formation, shown by weak brownish colouring or structure in the profile.

facts.text: Cambisols form in medium- and fine-textured material from many rock types, mostly in alluvial, colluvial and wind-blown deposits.
Most make good, intensively used farmland, and temperate Cambisols are among the most productive soils on earth.
They cover an estimated 15 million square kilometres worldwide.
They are widespread in temperate and boreal lands glaciated in the Pleistocene, where parent material is young and soil formation is slow.
In the tropics they are less common, appearing mainly where active erosion keeps soils young.
The weakly leached brown earths of Europe are Cambisols in the WRB; Poland's brown forest soils correspond to Cambisols and to USDA Udepts.

prerequisites: World Reference Base for Soil Resources

title: Chernozem

definition.text: A black soil, also called black earth or regur, with 4% to 16% humus and plenty of phosphorus and ammonia compounds; a WRB reference soil group.

facts.text: The name joins the Russian words for 'black' and 'earth'.
In the WRB key a Chernozem has a very dark, well-structured topsoil and secondary carbonates.
Chernozem is very fertile and holds much moisture, but long cropping still needs fertiliser because its humus, and with it its nutrients, steadily declines.
Dokuchaev studied the steppe soils of Poltava in 1883 and that year published Russian Chernozem, the first description of the soil in European Russia.
Chernozem covers about 230 million hectares in two belts: the Eurasian Steppe, and the Canadian Prairies south through the Great Plains to Kansas.
Its dark layer ranges from a few centimetres to 1.5 metres (60 inches) thick in Ukraine and the Red River Valley.
In the WRB the USDA Mollisols split into Chernozems, Kastanozems and Phaeozems, which together match Canada's Chernozemic order.
Ukraine banned farmland sales from 1992 to 2020, but trucked-away soil could be sold, feeding a black market put at about US$900 million a year in 2011.

prerequisites: World Reference Base for Soil Resources

title: Theories of chernozem origin

definition.text: The competing explanations, offered since 1763, for how chernozem's thick black topsoil formed.

facts.text: Early ideas ranged from decaying plants and animals (Lomonosov, 1763) and weathered Jurassic marine shales (Murchison, 1840) to marine sediments (1851) and decomposed steppe grasses (Ruprecht, 1866).
No single reconstruction of past climate explains the geochemical variation of central European chernozems; evidence of human-made pyrogenic carbon led to a burning theory (Schmidt, 1999).
Chernozem has the highest magnetic susceptibility of the major soil types; heat turns goethite and ferrihydrite into maghemite, pointing to fire, likely set by early humans.
Humification alone can darken soils, so 'chernozem' may cover black soils that look alike but formed in different ways.

contested_note: Sources propose humus build-up under steppe grass, marine sediments and prehistoric burning, and no single explanation fits all chernozems.

title: Durisol

definition.text: A WRB reference soil group of free-draining dryland soils whose grains are cemented by secondary silica in the upper metre, as nodules or as a continuous hardpan.

facts.text: The name comes from Latin durus, 'hard'; the cemented layer is called a duripan, hardpan in Australia or dorbank in South Africa.
Durisols form mainly in alluvial and colluvial deposits on plains, terraces and gentle piedmont slopes in arid, semi-arid and Mediterranean regions; erosion often exposes the hard layer.
Most are fit only for extensive grazing; crops need irrigation.
Large areas occur in Australia, South Africa, Namibia and the south-western United States, but as a new group they are rarely mapped and their extent is unknown.

prerequisites: World Reference Base for Soil Resources

title: Fluvisol

definition.text: A WRB reference soil group of genetically young, stratified soils in river, lake or marine sediments.

facts.text: Fluvisols occur on alluvial plains, river fans, valleys and tidal marshes on every continent and in every climate zone.
They show clear layering and weak horizons, and under natural conditions flood from time to time.
They correspond to the fluvents and fluvaquents of USDA soil taxonomy.
People recognised their natural fertility, and dry living sites on river levees, in prehistoric times.
Many dryland crops grow on them with water control, and paddy rice is widespread on irrigated and drained tropical Fluvisols.
Coastal Fluvisols with sulphidic material are acid sulfate soils, limited by low pH, toxic aluminium and salt; strongly saline tidal land is best left under mangroves.
Large areas lie along the Amazon, the Ganges plain and Lake Chad, and in deltas such as the Mekong, Mississippi and Nile.

prerequisites: World Reference Base for Soil Resources

title: Gleysol

definition.text: A WRB reference soil group of soils saturated by groundwater long enough, unless drained, to develop gleyic colours: grey or blue inside, rusty at ped surfaces.

facts.text: They are also called meadow soils, groundwater soils or Gleyzems, and match the Aqu- suborders of USDA Entisols, Inceptisols and Mollisols.
In the WRB, redox features from rising groundwater make a Gleysol, while those from stagnant surface water make a Stagnosol or Planosol.
Gleysols form in many unconsolidated sediments, mostly river, marine and lake deposits, in depressions and low positions with shallow groundwater.
They cover an estimated 720 million hectares, occur in nearly all climates, and are most extensive in northern Russia, Siberia, Canada, Alaska, China and Bangladesh.
About 200 million hectares lie in the tropics, mainly in the Amazon, equatorial Africa and the coastal swamps of Southeast Asia.
Drained Gleysols are used for arable crops, dairy farming and horticulture, and in the tropics and subtropics they are widely planted with rice.
Green rust, a layered iron(II)-iron(III) hydroxide, occurs in them as the mineral fougerite.

prerequisites: World Reference Base for Soil Resources
notes: Wetness-as-main-limitation sentence S:76ae1607cfe6 carries CITATION NEEDED and was not used.

title: Gypsisol

definition.text: A WRB reference soil group of soils with a substantial secondary accumulation of gypsum (CaSO4·2H2O).

facts.text: Gypsisols are confined to the driest arid lands, probably about 100 million hectares in all, around Mesopotamia, central Asia, the Libyan and Namib deserts, Australia and the south-western United States.
They are Gypsids in USDA soil taxonomy and Desert soils in the Russian classification.
Calcium sulphate, with or without carbonates, collects in and below the B horizon of soils formed in alluvial, colluvial and wind-blown deposits.
Deep Gypsisols near water can grow many crops, but a shallow petrogypsic horizon cuts yields, and gypsum dissolving in irrigation water makes the land subside unevenly, so canals must be lined.

prerequisites: World Reference Base for Soil Resources

title: Kastanozem

definition.text: A WRB reference soil group, also called chestnut soil, with a dark, humus-rich topsoil and secondary carbonates.

facts.text: Kastanozems are paler than Chernozems and relate to the Mollisols of USDA soil taxonomy.
Native grassland gave them a brown surface layer within the first metre, a high level of exchangeable calcium and secondary carbonates starting within 70 cm of the mineral surface.
They occupy relatively dry zones receiving 200 to 450 mm of rain a year.
The name comes from the Russian and Latin words for chestnut, after the colour of its husk.

prerequisites: World Reference Base for Soil Resources

title: Leptosol

definition.text: A WRB reference soil group of very shallow soils over continuous rock, or deeper soils packed with gravel and stones.

facts.text: Leptosols cover about 1.7 billion hectares, from the tropics to polar regions and from sea level to the highest peaks.
They are widespread in mountains, notably in Asia, South America, northern Canada and Alaska, and in the Saharan and Arabian deserts.
Elsewhere they occur on hard rock or where erosion has kept pace with soil formation or stripped the topsoil.
Lithic Leptosols, less than 10 cm deep, in mountain regions are the most extensive Leptosols on Earth.
The 1974 FAO legend called Leptosols on limestone Rendzinas and those on acid rock Rankers; in the WRB a rendzina may key out as a Leptosol, Chernozem, Kastanozem or Phaeozem.
They hold little water, so are poor for rainfed farming, though some suit tree crops or extensive grazing.
Many USDA orthents, and shallow or gravelly Mollisols, belong to the Leptosols.

prerequisites: World Reference Base for Soil Resources

title: Lixisol

definition.text: A WRB reference soil group of soils with a subsurface build-up of low-activity clays and high base saturation, where base cations equal or exceed exchangeable aluminium.

facts.text: Lixisols develop under intense tropical weathering in subhumid to semi-arid climates.
Most USDA Alfisols are Luvisols or Lixisols in the WRB.
With Acrisols they are the FAO groups of tropical climates with clay-enriched layers, and in Amazonia they are among the natural soils too poor in minerals to resupply nutrients.

prerequisites: World Reference Base for Soil Resources

title: Luvisol

definition.text: A WRB reference soil group with a clay-enriched subsoil of high-activity clays, in which base cations equal or exceed exchangeable aluminium.

facts.text: Their defining feature is an argic horizon, a subsurface layer with more clay than the material above, formed as water washes clay downward.
The clays are little weathered, high-activity 2:1 types, giving high cation exchange capacity and high base saturation.
Where uneroded, a paler, clay-depleted eluvial horizon lies above the argic horizon.
Luvisols cover 500–600 million hectares, mainly in temperate zones, form on many parent materials, and are generally fertile and widely farmed.
In Mediterranean regions hematite colours them red as Chromic Luvisols; such duplex soils with strong wet-dry seasons are called calcic and chromic luvisols.
In USDA soil taxonomy most are Alfisols; Canada's system also has Luvisols, whose clay-enriched Bt horizon forms mainly by lessivage.

prerequisites: World Reference Base for Soil Resources

title: Nitisol

definition.text: A WRB reference soil group of deep, red, well-drained tropical soils with at least 30% clay and a strong polyhedral or blocky structure.

facts.text: The clay-rich layer extends as deep as 150 cm, and its blocky aggregates show shiny pressure faces, shaped by iron oxides and high water content.
Nitisols form from fine material weathered from intermediate to basic rock; kaolinite, halloysite and iron oxides dominate, and they fix phosphorus.
They occur in the tropics and subtropics, extensively in the highlands of Ethiopia, Kenya, the DR Congo and Cameroon.
They correlate with kandic Alfisols, Ultisols and Inceptisols of USDA soil taxonomy.

prerequisites: World Reference Base for Soil Resources

title: Phaeozem

definition.text: A WRB reference soil group of dark soils with a high base status but no secondary carbonates within one metre of the surface.

facts.text: Most Phaeozems match the Udolls, a suborder of the Mollisols in USDA soil taxonomy.
They form on loess and glacial till under humid and sub-humid tall-grass steppe, with extensive areas in the United States, Argentina and China.
They typically hold about 5% organic matter and have a pH of 5–7.
They are farmed intensively for wheat, soybean and cotton and as improved cattle pasture.

prerequisites: World Reference Base for Soil Resources

title: Planosol

definition.text: A WRB reference soil group with a pale, coarse-textured topsoil showing periodic water stagnation that abruptly overlies a dense, slowly permeable, much more clayey subsoil.

facts.text: The abrupt texture change comes from layered deposits or from clay destruction and removal; water perched above it creates temporary reducing conditions and a stagnic colour pattern.
The 1938 US classification used the name Planosols; USDA soil taxonomy now puts most in the Albaqualfs, Albaquults and Argialbolls.
They cover about 130 million hectares of seasonally waterlogged flats in subtropical and temperate regions with marked wet and dry seasons.
Oxygen shortage when wet, dense subsoil and sometimes toxic aluminium hamper roots, so most are grazed and yields stay modest, though Southeast Asia grows paddy rice on them.

prerequisites: World Reference Base for Soil Resources

title: Plinthosol

definition.text: A WRB reference soil group defined by plinthite, petroplinthite or pisoliths, iron-oxide concretions, in a plinthic horizon starting within 50 cm of the surface.

facts.text: They form in wet-dry tropics where water tables rise and fall: saturated soil reduces and mobilises iron, which on drying precipitates as ferric oxides in mottled patterns.
Plinthite, a red clay-rich material rich in iron oxides, sometimes over 80%, hardens irreversibly into ironstone with repeated wetting and drying.
Fertility is low; bottomlands waterlog, shallow areas suffer drought, and shallow petroplinthite often leaves only grazing, though cocoa and cashew are grown in places.
Soils with plinthite cover about 60 million hectares; soft plinthite dominates the humid Amazon and Congo basins, while hardened caps cover drier Sudano-Sahelian landforms.

prerequisites: World Reference Base for Soil Resources

title: Podzol

definition.text: An acid soil with an organic topsoil over a bleached, ash-grey leached layer and an iron-, aluminium- or humus-enriched subsoil; the typical soil of boreal and coniferous forests.

facts.text: Podzols, also called podosols, spodosols or espodossolos, also typify eucalypt forests and heathlands of southern Australia.
The name is Russian for 'under-ash', given by Dokuchaev in 1875 after peasants who ploughed up what looked like a layer of ash on first breaking such soils.
Under 5 to 10 cm of decomposing litter lies an E horizon, usually 4 to 8 cm thick and poor in iron and aluminium oxides and humus, over a red or red-brown podzolic B horizon.
Podzolization makes them: dissolved organic matter, iron and aluminium form chelates that percolating water carries from the E to the B horizon, sometimes cementing a hardpan called ortstein.
They form mostly on quartz-rich sands, sandstone or debris of magmatic rock under high rainfall, in cool humid climates where slow decay lets acid mor layers build up.
Most are poor farmland, sandy, short of water and nutrients, acidic, phosphate-deficient and aluminium-toxic; grazing suits them best, though limed and fertilised loamy types can crop well.
Podzols cover about 4,850,000 square kilometres, mostly in temperate and boreal zones of the Northern Hemisphere.
USDA and Chinese taxonomy call them Spodosols; Canada matches them with its Podzolic order, Australia uses Podosols and Brazil Espodossolos.

notes: Podzolization itself is the how-soils-form seed 'Podsolisation'; this entry only summarises it. 'Spodosol' redirects to Podzol, so this entry also stands for the USDA Spodosols.

title: Regosol

definition.text: A WRB reference soil group of very weakly developed mineral soils in unconsolidated material, with no significant profile development.

facts.text: Regosols are a leftover group for soils that fit no other; weakly developed soils that qualify as Leptosols, Arenosols or Fluvisols are excluded.
Their profiles stay minimal because they are young or form slowly, and they are extensive in eroding lands, especially arid and semi-arid areas and mountains.
They cover about 260 million hectares, mainly in arid areas of the mid-western United States, northern Africa, the Near East and Australia.
They match USDA Entisols and Australian Rudosols; most are lightly grazed, some are irrigated intensively, and mountain Regosols are best left under forest.

prerequisites: World Reference Base for Soil Resources

title: Retisol

definition.text: A WRB reference soil group in which a pale, clay-poor eluvial horizon tongues in a net-like pattern into the darker, clay-rich argic horizon below.

facts.text: The interfingering is called retic properties, from Latin rete, 'net'.
Retisols entered the WRB in its third edition in 2014, absorbing the more narrowly defined Albeluvisols of 1998 and 2006; they resemble the FAO's Podzoluvisols.
They occur mainly in former periglacial areas of the last glaciation in Europe and North America, along a belt from Belgium to Russia, rarely over large areas.
Water drains through the clay-poor tongues while the dense, nutrient-richer clay parts are often too dry and hard to root; earthworms avoid them and most are forest or pasture.

prerequisites: World Reference Base for Soil Resources

title: WRB argic soil groups
article: Retisol#Relationships with other Reference Soil Groups

definition.text: The five WRB reference soil groups that must have an argic, clay-enriched subsoil horizon: Retisols, Acrisols, Lixisols, Alisols and Luvisols.

facts.text: Only Retisols have retic properties; the other four are separated by the cation exchange capacity per kg of clay in the argic horizon and by the subsoil's effective base saturation.
Acrisols have low-activity clays with more exchangeable aluminium than base cations; Lixisols have low-activity clays with base cations at least equal to aluminium.
Alisols have high-activity clays dominated by aluminium; Luvisols have high-activity clays with base cations at least equal to aluminium.
A soil with an argic horizon and retic properties dominated by stagnant water is classed instead as a Retic Stagnosol.
Most USDA Alfisols become Luvisols or Lixisols, and most Ultisols become Acrisols or Alisols.

prerequisites: World Reference Base for Soil Resources
notes: A two-by-two grid (low/high clay activity against aluminium/base-cation dominance) could be drawn from the WRB list lines; no image needed.

title: Solonchak

definition.text: A WRB reference soil group of pale or grey, poorly drained soils of arid to subhumid lands with high concentrations of soluble salts.

facts.text: The word is Russian for 'salt marsh', from sol, 'salt'.
Most USDA Aridisols fall into the WRB's Calcisols, Gypsisols, Durisols and Solonchaks.
Many Calcisols lie next to Solonchaks that are really salt-affected Calcisols.
Solonetz zones are associated with Gleysols, Solonchaks and Kastanozems.
Irrigation with saline groundwater has caused catastrophic salinisation and Solonchak formation, as in Central Asia.

prerequisites: World Reference Base for Soil Resources
notes: The Solonchak page is a three-sentence stub; most facts come from other pages.

title: Solonetz

definition.text: A WRB reference soil group with a clay-enriched subsoil high in exchangeable sodium, the natric horizon, within the upper 100 cm.

facts.text: The natric horizon, named from Latin natrium, 'sodium', has more clay than the layer above and over 15% exchangeable sodium.
The name comes from Russian sol, 'salt'; the Ukrainian folk word solontsi means salty soil, and many Ukrainian villages bear it.
Solonetz zones go with Gleysols, Solonchaks and Kastanozems.
In USDA soil taxonomy Solonetz are sodium-rich Alfisols; Alfisols and Mollisols with a natric horizon key out as Solonetz.
In Canada such soils develop from saline parent material to Solonetz, Solodized Solonetz and Solod as leaching removes salts, until the sodic B horizon may disintegrate.
Solonetz is one of the Russian soil terms, with chernozem, podzol and gley, that Dokuchaev's work brought into international use.

prerequisites: World Reference Base for Soil Resources

title: Stagnosol

definition.text: A WRB reference soil group with strong mottling caused by redox processes under stagnating surface water, without a marked texture change.

facts.text: Periodically wet, they are mottled in topsoil and subsoil, sometimes with concretions or a fully bleached albic topsoil; many national systems call them pseudogley.
They cover 150–200 million hectares, mostly on flat to gently sloping land in humid temperate West and Central Europe, North America, south-east Australia and Argentina.
Water stagnating above a dense subsoil starves roots of oxygen, and unlike Gleysols they often need deep loosening or ploughing, not just drains; once drained they can be fertile.
Many are Aqualfs, Aquults, Aquents, Aquepts or Aquolls in USDA soil taxonomy.

prerequisites: World Reference Base for Soil Resources
notes: The Stagnosol lead's last two sentences (S:5ef7efdab7b8, S:d182e5eaa1c6) repeat Planosol text, an apparent copy-paste error on the page; not used.

title: Technosol

definition.text: A WRB reference soil group of soils whose properties and formation are dominated by their technical, human-made origin.

facts.text: A Technosol holds a significant amount of artefacts, has a geotechnical liner, or is sealed by technic hard material unlike natural rock.
They include soils of landfills, sludge, cinders, mine spoil and ash, pavements with their underlying material, and constructed soils; merely transported natural soil does not count.
Often called urban or mine soils, they occur near cities, roads, mines, dumps, oil spills and fly-ash deposits, usually in small patches.
A Technosol can differentiate A and O horizons at more than one centimetre per year.
They are more likely than other soils to be contaminated, and many must be handled with care because of toxic industrial substances.
Some are made on purpose to cover wastes such as mine tailings, as at Andacollo in Chile.
They are closely related to Anthrosols, soils created by long-term measures to raise fertility for farming.

prerequisites: World Reference Base for Soil Resources

title: Umbrisol

definition.text: A WRB reference soil group with a dark, organic-rich mineral topsoil of low base saturation.

facts.text: Umbrisols are the low-base counterpart of Chernozems, Kastanozems and Phaeozems, and develop in weathered siliceous rock.
They cover about 100 million hectares, above the tree line in the Andes, Himalaya and Central Asia, and lower down in cleared northern and western Europe and on North America's Pacific seaboard.
Slopes and wet, cool climate restrict most to extensive grazing improved by better grasses and liming, and many erode easily; in New Zealand they became productive sheep and dairy land.
USDA soil taxonomy places such soils in great groups of Entisols and Inceptisols, and British brown podzolic soils are Umbrisols in the WRB.

prerequisites: World Reference Base for Soil Resources
notes: Climate sentence S:3774ec171f6f carries CITATION NEEDED and was not used.

title: Albeluvisols

definition.text: A former WRB reference soil group (1998 and 2006 editions): soils with a thin dark topsoil over a bleached albic horizon that tongues into a clay-enriched Bt horizon.

facts.text: The third edition of the WRB in 2014 replaced them with the more broadly defined Retisols.
They correlate with the Glossaqualfs, Glossocryalfs and Glossudalfs of USDA soil taxonomy.
They formed in glacial till, lake and river deposits or loess on plains under coniferous or mixed forest, and cover an estimated 320 million hectares, mostly on former Pleistocene permafrost.
Acidity, few nutrients and tillage and drainage problems limit farming, so those of the northern taiga are almost all forest.

prerequisites: World Reference Base for Soil Resources
notes: Superseded group kept as its own entry because it has its own article; FAO 'Podzoluvisols' redirects here.

title: Aridity

definition.text: The condition of regions with low annual precipitation, high temperatures and little available water.

facts.text: Arid areas make up about 43% of the world's land and tend to have degraded soils.
Where aridity falls depends mainly on the general circulation of the atmosphere, which shifts with climate change; land-use change can also raise the demand on soil water.
A December 2024 UNCCD report found that over three-quarters of Earth's land has become permanently drier in recent decades, and a quarter of people live in expanding drylands.
Desertification is a gradual rise in soil aridity, and warming-driven aridity also adds to the salinisation of waterlogged soils.

notes: Assigned page. The Nile Basin sentence S:1f197d0e7a13 gives a temperature rise of '1.5–2.1 percent', an odd unit for temperature; not used.

definition.text: A deep, humus-rich anthropogenic soil, or plaggic Anthrosol, built up on poor podzols of north-west Europe from the Middle Ages by plaggen farming.

facts.text: Farmers cut sods of heath or grass with roots and humus, used them as bedding for cattle or sheep, then spread the slurry-soaked bedding on fields in spring as manure.
Centuries of this built fertile soil 40 cm to over 1.50 m deep, against about 30 cm for modern arable soils, raising fields with sharp edges called Plaggenesche in Germany or Es in Dutch.
The practice ended around 1900 with the arrival of fertilisers, though Orkney had such soils by the 12th to 13th centuries and parts of Shetland kept the method until the 1960s.
Maori farmers in New Zealand used plaggen-like practices to improve drainage for kumara.

title: Black Dirt Region

definition.text: A drained former marsh in Orange County, New York, and Sussex County, New Jersey, named for its dark, extremely fertile sapric muck soil.

facts.text: The muck formed on an ancient glacial lake bed, enriched by decades of Wallkill River floods; its 26,000 acres (10,400 ha) are the largest such tract in the US outside the Everglades.
Early settlers avoided the flood-prone land; a drainage canal was dug in 1835, and Polish and Volga German immigrants used to similar soils began farming it.
Its black dirt onions averaged 30,000 lb/acre (3.4 kg/m2) by the late 20th century; farmers now also grow vegetables, sod, hemp and cannabis.
The muck is poor ground for building, so development of the farmland is considered unlikely.

notes: Assigned regional page (one US district); kept as a Minor worked example of a drained organic muck soil. Drainage-date sentence S:82f60f002d5d (around 1880) carries CITATION NEEDED and was not used.

title: Water stagnation

definition.text: The condition of water that has stopped flowing for a long time.

facts.text: Stagnant water favours anaerobic bacteria, and as little as six days of stagnation can completely change its bacterial community.

notes: Assigned page, but it covers stagnant water bodies and their health hazards, not stagnant water in soils; the soil sense is taught by Stagnosol, Planosol and Gleying.

title: WRB qualifiers

definition.text: The principal and supplementary qualifiers that the WRB adds to a Reference Soil Group name to describe a soil further.

facts.text: Principal qualifiers are ranked by importance, reflecting major subdivisions of the group or properties that strongly affect how the soil functions; they precede the group name.
Supplementary qualifiers describe additional traits, are not ranked and follow the name in brackets: texture first, the rest alphabetically.
Chapter 4 of the WRB manual lists, for every group, the principal and supplementary qualifiers available.
The worked example becomes an Albic Stagnic Luvisol (Siltic, Loamic, Aric, Cutanic, Differentic, Endic, Ochric).

prerequisites: Naming a soil with the WRB
